item.title: Turning Quantum Uncertainty Into Precision Quantum Sensing
item.description:
Turning Quantum Uncertainty Into Precision Quantum Sensing pro Wed, 14/10/2026 - 12:27

Turning Quantum Uncertainty Into Precision Quantum Sensing 
IIT Bombay researchers show how engineered light interacting with graphene can measure elusive quantum phenomena.
 

 Image credits : Google Gemini

 

 

Voltage fluctuations, light fluctuations, temperature fluctuations—any fluctuations are troublesome and thus undesirable. They don’t just cause discomfort; in engineering and medical applications, they affect the accuracy of measurements or introduce errors in controls. Even at the minute level of quantum phenomena, fluctuations are considered undesirable. But what if some fluctuations can be made useful? A theoretical study from the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay (IIT Bombay) shows that structured quantum fluctuations in light can be used to sense and generate useful quantum optical signals.

Mr Kartik Prabhu and Prof Gopal Dixit of IIT Bombay's Physics Department have proposed a new way to detect quantum fluctuations in light using the quantum material graphene as a sensor. Their study, published in the American Physical Society journal Physical Review B Letter, shows that when specially prepared quantum light is shone on graphene, its interaction with graphene can reveal information about the quantum nature of the incident light. It also shows that by carefully engineering the quantum fluctuations in the incident light, we can generate tailored high-frequency emission. 

“Our study brings together, for the first time, quantum light, a quantum material and high harmonic generation in the extreme ultraviolet frequency range”, says Prof Gopal Dixit. High harmonic generation is an emerging technique for imaging electron dynamics and makes it possible to even track complex chemical reactions in real time. The method, for which the Nobel Prize in Physics for the year 2023 was awarded, involves shining short, intense laser pulses on noble gases or specific solids to obtain a very short pulse of attosecond duration (billionth billionth part of a second) with a frequency an exact integer multiple of the original laser’s frequency. 


Quantum fluctuations in light

In classical physics, light is treated as a wave and described by its intensity (amplitude) and the initial shift of the wave's peaks (phase). As we scale down to minute levels in time, space, and intensity, we enter the realm of quantum physics. Here, light is described in terms of intensity and phase values, with a range of uncertainty for both.

Even in a complete vacuum or total darkness, there are temporary random changes in the amount of energy at a point. Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle states that two quantities with specific mathematical relationships cannot be known with absolute precision. For example, we can precisely determine either a particle's position or its momentum, but not both at the same time.

The uncertainty is present in light too. These disturbances due to the uncertainty are termed quantum fluctuations. This uncertainty limits highly sensitive measurements, such as atomic clocks (which keep time by measuring atomic vibrations) or gravitational-wave measurements at LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory).

For laser light, the uncertainty, or quantum fluctuations, are spread equally between intensity and phase. In a diagram where the x-axis represents intensity and the y-axis represents phase, the equally distributed quantum fluctuations form an uncertainty circle.

You can reduce the uncertainty of one parameter at the cost of increasing the uncertainty of the other by passing laser light through specific materials called non-linear crystals. In the phase-intensity graph, the perfect circle would get squished in one direction and elongated in the other. Such light is called squeezed light.

Sensing quantum fluctuations

The IIT Bombay study considers graphene illuminated by light with two circularly polarised frequency components rotating in opposite directions, with one component's frequency twice the other's. The light interacts with graphene to generate high-frequency light, with frequencies several times higher than the incident light (high harmonic generation). For light with no enhanced quantum fluctuations, some high-harmonic frequencies can be produced, and some (specifically multiples of 3 times the fundamental frequency of the incident light) are forbidden.

When the researchers consider that the driving light is in a squeezed quantum state (it has enhanced quantum fluctuations), the results show that the quantum fluctuations activate signals that would otherwise be forbidden. Theoretical analysis revealed that the quantum fluctuations affect the polarisation of the emitted light. The researchers considered different variations and combinations of the incident-light parameters and analysed the spectrum of the emitted light. They found that each combination produced emitted light with specific characteristics, indicating that the emitted light can be used to sense specific properties of the incident light.

While basic mathematical processing of the emitted light could reveal which frequency component of the incident light carried quantum fluctuations, it did not reveal information about the quantum component itself. To uncover information about the quantum fluctuations, the researchers further analysed the data. They showed that the forbidden frequency components of the emitted light carry distinct information about the intensity and polarisation of the quantum fluctuations in the incident light. This information provides an experimentally observable parameter for detecting quantum fluctuations in the incident light.

“An important feature of the proposed approach is its ultrafast nature. High-harmonic generation occurs within a fraction of an optical cycle, allowing the interaction between quantum light and matter to be explored on extremely short timescales,” says Prof Dixit.

Although the present study focuses on graphene, the underlying idea may be relevant to a broader class of quantum materials and nonlinear optical systems. Going ahead, Prof Dixit plans to explore different quantum materials. Generating datasets to train a machine learning model and apply AI to generalise the concept is also on the cards.

item.title: Ground-breaking ceremony of the Biodiversity Lab at Soneri Baug
item.description:
Ground-breaking ceremony of the Biodiversity Lab at Soneri Baug tejaswi.kamath Tue, 13/10/2026 - 10:45

On 8th October 2026, IIT Bombay marked an important milestone with the ground-breaking ceremony for phase-I of the Biodiversity Lab at Soneri Baug, located along the lakeside fringe road on the campus.

The event was graced by many Institute functionaries and representatives from the Estate Office, Chief Security Office, Facility Management office and Public Health Office. Dean (IPS) shared his perspectives on integrating environmental considerations into campus development.

Envisaged as a living laboratory for research, learning and restoration, Biodiversity Lab reflects IIT Bombay's commitment to understanding and conserving its natural heritage, while creating a more sustainable campus.
